corrections.notes: Guidelines start aspirin at 12-16 weeks (NICE from 12 weeks; ideally before 16 weeks). Keyed 16-20 weeks is too late.
corrections.source: NICE NG133 (2019); USPSTF 2021 aspirin for preeclampsia prevention
corrections.newExplanation: Chronic hypertension is a high-risk factor for pre-eclampsia, so low-dose aspirin is advised. NICE recommends starting from 12 weeks' gestation, and guidelines advise starting before 16 weeks where possible. Starting at 16-20 weeks is later than recommended. Source: NICE NG133 (2019); USPSTF 2021 aspirin for preeclampsia prevention

corrections.notes: OCA is no longer available for PBC (EMA revoked 2024; US withdrawal 2025). Second-line now is a PPAR agonist (elafibranor/seladelpar) or bezafibrate.
corrections.source: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines on PBC (2025); FDA accelerated approvals of elafibranor and seladelpar (2024)
corrections.newExplanation: Patients with an inadequate biochemical response to UDCA need second-line add-on therapy. Obeticholic acid is no longer available for PBC (EU authorisation revoked in 2024, US marketing withdrawn), so current options are the PPAR agonists elafibranor or seladelpar, or off-label bezafibrate, continued alongside UDCA. Corticosteroids and azathioprine have no role in PBC alone. Source: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines on PBC (2025); FDA accelerated approvals of elafibranor and seladelpar (2024)

optionEdits.after: Add a PPAR agonist (elafibranor or seladelpar) or bezafibrate

corrections.notes: Listing urgency for PSC transplant is MELD-based (AASLD 2022), with exception points for recurrent cholangitis; the Mayo PSC risk score is a natural-history tool, not the listing standard. Explanation admits weak support.
corrections.source: AASLD PSC practice guidance 2022
corrections.newExplanation: Transplant listing priority in PSC follows the MELD score, as for other causes of cirrhosis; exception points may be considered for complications such as recurrent cholangitis. The Mayo PSC risk score estimates natural history but is not the listing standard. Source: AASLD PSC practice guidance 2022

corrections.notes: Symptomatic PSP of 2.5 cm: the linked BTS 2010 guideline recommends needle aspiration (14-16G) first-line, with a chest drain only if aspiration fails. BTS 2023 also allows conservative management or ambulatory devices.
corrections.source: BTS Pleural Disease Guideline 2023 (pneumothorax); BTS 2010
corrections.newExplanation: Symptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax with a 2.5 cm rim needs intervention. BTS guidance supports needle aspiration (or an ambulatory device) as first-line, with a small-bore chest drain if aspiration fails. Proceeding straight to a chest drain is not first-line, and VATS is for recurrence or persistent air leak. Source: BTS Pleural Disease Guideline 2023 (pneumothorax); BTS 2010

corrections.notes: The linked IDSA 2013 PJI guideline advises withholding antibiotics for at least 2 weeks before aspiration/biopsy, when clinically stable, to improve culture yield. Keyed B contradicts it.
corrections.source: IDSA prosthetic joint infection guideline 2013 (linked)
corrections.newExplanation: IDSA advises withholding antibiotics for at least 2 weeks before aspiration or tissue sampling for suspected PJI, when the patient is clinically stable, to improve culture yield. Continuing antibiotics risks culture-negative infection and untargeted treatment. Source: IDSA prosthetic joint infection guideline 2013 (linked)

corrections.notes: UPCR 0.8 at 3 weeks is not remission (<=0.2). IPNA 2023: continue daily prednisolone to complete 4 weeks (up to 6 if no remission) before alternate-day taper. Tapering now (C) is premature. Explanation admits weak support.
corrections.source: IPNA 2023 recommendations for steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome
corrections.newExplanation: A UPCR of 0.8 mg/mg is improved but is not yet remission. IPNA recommends continuing daily prednisolone for the initial phase, extended up to 6 weeks if remission has not been reached, before the alternate-day taper. Tapering now would be premature and stopping abruptly risks relapse. Source: IPNA 2023 recommendations for steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome

corrections.notes: Muddled stem (eradication vs exacerbation). For a mild outpatient exacerbation with known Pseudomonas, BTS/ERS treat with oral ciprofloxacin for 14 days. Inhaled tobramycin is long-term suppression, not initial management.
corrections.source: BTS bronchiectasis guideline 2019; ERS bronchiectasis guideline 2017
corrections.newExplanation: For a mild exacerbation in bronchiectasis with Pseudomonas aeruginosa that can be managed as an outpatient, BTS and ERS recommend oral ciprofloxacin for 14 days, which is also first-line eradication therapy. Inhaled tobramycin is a long-term suppressive option for chronic infection, not the initial treatment. Source: BTS bronchiectasis guideline 2019; ERS bronchiectasis guideline 2017

corrections.notes: Headache, focal deficit and seizure point to a paradoxical embolic complication, especially brain abscess or stroke (C). PAVM haemorrhage in pregnancy causes haemoptysis/haemothorax, not focal neurology.
corrections.source: BTS clinical statement on pulmonary AVMs 2017 (linked)
corrections.newExplanation: Headache, focal neurological deficit and seizure in a patient with a PAVM point to a paradoxical embolic complication, especially cerebral abscess or stroke, caused by right-to-left shunting. Haemorrhage from a PAVM in pregnancy presents as haemoptysis or haemothorax, not focal neurology. Source: BTS clinical statement on pulmonary AVMs 2017 (linked)

corrections.notes: Intermediate-high-risk PE: ESC 2019 recommends anticoagulation with monitoring and rescue reperfusion only if haemodynamic decompensation. Routine catheter-directed thrombolysis isn't standard (PEITHO; trials ongoing).
corrections.source: ESC acute pulmonary embolism guideline 2019
corrections.newExplanation: Normotensive PE with RV dysfunction and raised troponin is intermediate-high risk. ESC recommends therapeutic anticoagulation with close monitoring, reserving rescue reperfusion (systemic thrombolysis, or catheter-directed therapy/surgery as alternatives) for haemodynamic decompensation. Routine primary reperfusion is not recommended. Source: ESC acute pulmonary embolism guideline 2019

corrections.notes: Radial arteries are typically 2-3 mm; "<5 mm is inadequate" is false (a 6F sheath needs about 2.5 mm). Severe PAD argues against femoral access, so radial remains preferred.
corrections.source: ESC NSTE-ACS 2020 and ESC ACS 2023 guidelines (radial access preferred)
corrections.newExplanation: Radial access is the recommended default for PCI, and a radial artery of about 3 mm is normal and usually adequate. Severe peripheral artery disease makes femoral access more hazardous, which is a further reason to prefer the radial route here. Source: ESC NSTE-ACS 2020 and ESC ACS 2023 guidelines (radial access preferred)

corrections.notes: In haemorrhagic shock, transfusion is driven by bleeding and perfusion (major haemorrhage protocol), not by targeting Hb 9-10. D is the best answer.
corrections.source: European guideline on management of major bleeding and coagulopathy following trauma; NICE NG24 blood transfusion
corrections.newExplanation: In haemorrhagic shock, transfusion is driven by ongoing bleeding and signs of inadequate perfusion, managed with a major haemorrhage protocol, rather than by a haemoglobin threshold or target. Haemoglobin lags behind blood loss in acute haemorrhage. Source: European guideline on management of major bleeding and coagulopathy following trauma; NICE NG24 blood transfusion

corrections.notes: Relapse at 8 months (<12 months) is early relapse, where second-line CAR-T (axi-cel, ZUMA-7; NICE TA895) is now standard over salvage plus ASCT.
corrections.source: ZUMA-7 (Locke et al, NEJM 2022); NICE TA895
corrections.newExplanation: Relapse within 12 months of first-line R-CHOP is early relapse. In ZUMA-7, second-line axicabtagene ciloleucel improved event-free survival over salvage chemotherapy plus autologous transplant in this group, and CAR T-cell therapy is now the standard second-line option for fit patients with early relapse. Salvage chemotherapy plus ASCT is reserved for later relapse. Source: ZUMA-7 (Locke et al, NEJM 2022); NICE TA895

optionEdits.after: Refer for second-line CAR T-cell therapy (e.g. axicabtagene ciloleucel)

corrections.notes: RAVE: complete remission at 6 months was 64% with rituximab (vs 53% CYC), within 60-70%, not 70-80%.
corrections.source: RAVE trial (Stone et al, NEJM 2010)
corrections.newExplanation: In RAVE, the primary endpoint (complete remission off prednisone at 6 months) was reached by 64% of patients on rituximab versus 53% on cyclophosphamide, showing rituximab was non-inferior. This sits in the 60-70% band. Source: RAVE trial (Stone et al, NEJM 2010)

corrections.notes: Azathioprine as first-line maintenance is superseded: EULAR 2022/KDIGO 2024 prefer rituximab (MAINRITSAN). Explanation cites IBD/IgG4 reviews.
corrections.source: EULAR recommendations for AAV 2022; KDIGO 2024 ANCA vasculitis guideline; MAINRITSAN trial
corrections.newExplanation: After remission induction in AAV, EULAR 2022 and KDIGO 2024 recommend rituximab as the preferred maintenance agent, based on MAINRITSAN, which showed fewer major relapses with rituximab than with azathioprine. Azathioprine or methotrexate remain alternatives. Source: EULAR recommendations for AAV 2022; KDIGO 2024 ANCA vasculitis guideline; MAINRITSAN trial

optionEdits.after: Rituximab is generally preferred as the first-line maintenance agent after induction of remission.

corrections.notes: EULAR 2009 recommended at least 18 months, not 24; current EULAR 2022 advises 24-48 months. Question attributes the figure to superseded guidance.
corrections.source: EULAR recommendations for AAV 2022
corrections.stemFix: A 72-year-old patient with long-standing PR3-ANCA positive Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA) is in remission. She is currently on azathioprine for maintenance therapy. According to the 2022 EULAR recommendations, what is the recommended duration of maintenance immunosuppression for patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis in remission?
corrections.newExplanation: EULAR 2022 recommends continuing remission-maintenance therapy for 24 to 48 months after remission is achieved, with longer treatment considered in patients at higher relapse risk such as those with PR3-ANCA or previous relapse. The earlier 2009 recommendation of at least 18 months is superseded. Source: EULAR recommendations for AAV 2022

optionEdits.after: 24 to 48 months after remission

corrections.notes: Linked J Hypertens 2009 favours angiography; current ESC (2017 PAD/2024) recommend duplex ultrasound (or CTA/MRA) first-line, with DSA reserved for intervention.
corrections.source: ESC guidelines on peripheral arterial diseases 2017/2024
corrections.newExplanation: Current ESC guidance recommends duplex ultrasound as the first-line imaging test for suspected renal artery stenosis, with CT or MR angiography as alternatives. Catheter angiography is reserved for patients in whom revascularisation is being considered, rather than as the initial diagnostic test. Source: ESC guidelines on peripheral arterial diseases 2017/2024

corrections.notes: AASM 2024 recommends alpha-2-delta ligands (gabapentin/pregabalin) first-line and advises against standard use of dopamine agonists because of augmentation. Stem lacks a question lead-in.
corrections.source: AASM clinical practice guideline for RLS 2024
corrections.stemFix: A 62-year-old woman presents with daily irresistible urges to move her legs, accompanied by uncomfortable sensations, primarily in the evenings and at night. These symptoms are relieved by movement but recur upon rest, significantly disrupting her sleep. She has no significant medical history or medications. Her serum ferritin and transferrin saturation are above the thresholds for iron therapy. What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological treatment?
corrections.newExplanation: The AASM 2024 guideline recommends alpha-2-delta ligands (gabapentin enacarbil, gabapentin or pregabalin) as first-line drug treatment for RLS when iron therapy is not indicated. It advises against standard use of dopamine agonists such as pramipexole because of the risk of augmentation with long-term use. Benzodiazepines are not recommended. Source: AASM clinical practice guideline for RLS 2024

corrections.notes: AASM 2024 no longer supports dopamine agonists as first-line (conditional recommendation against standard use); alpha-2-delta ligands are preferred (not offered).
corrections.source: AASM clinical practice guideline for RLS 2024
corrections.newExplanation: The AASM 2024 guideline recommends alpha-2-delta ligands as first-line pharmacological treatment for RLS, after checking iron status. Dopamine agonists are no longer recommended for standard use because of augmentation, a progressive worsening of symptoms with long-term treatment. Source: AASM clinical practice guideline for RLS 2024

optionEdits.after: Alpha-2-delta ligands (gabapentin, pregabalin)

corrections.notes: TEAR found step-up from MTX monotherapy as effective as immediate combination by 2 years (immediate combination only faster at 24 weeks); "superior remission and slower progression" misstates it.
corrections.source: TEAR trial (Moreland et al, Arthritis Rheum 2012)
corrections.newExplanation: TEAR found that starting methotrexate monotherapy and stepping up to combination therapy if needed at 24 weeks gave outcomes comparable to immediate combination therapy over 2 years, including radiographic progression. Immediate combination was only better at the early time point. Source: TEAR trial (Moreland et al, Arthritis Rheum 2012)

corrections.notes: EULAR 2022: initial strategy is MTX plus short-term glucocorticoids, not routine initial combination with another csDMARD/bDMARD.
corrections.source: EULAR RA management recommendations 2022 (linked EULAR guidance)
corrections.newExplanation: EULAR recommends methotrexate as the first strategy in early RA, combined with short-term glucocorticoids, tapered and stopped as soon as clinically possible. Routine initial combination with another csDMARD or a bDMARD is not recommended. Source: EULAR RA management recommendations 2022 (linked EULAR guidance)

corrections.notes: Treat-to-target: assess at 3 months and escalate if no improvement; concurrent initial combination isn't recommended (EULAR 2022).
corrections.source: EULAR RA management recommendations 2022
corrections.newExplanation: Treat-to-target means starting methotrexate and reassessing: if there is no improvement by 3 months, or the target is not reached by 6 months, therapy is escalated. Starting a second agent at the same time as methotrexate is not the recommended default. Source: EULAR RA management recommendations 2022

corrections.notes: EULAR 2022/ACR 2021: start MTX (plus short-term GC) in DMARD-naive RA, reassess at 3 months, and add a b/tsDMARD only after csDMARD failure with poor prognostic factors. Routine upfront TNFi plus MTX isn't standard.
corrections.source: EULAR RA management recommendations 2022; ACR RA guideline 2021
corrections.newExplanation: In DMARD-naive RA, guidelines recommend starting methotrexate (often with short-term glucocorticoid bridging) and reassessing at about 3 months. A biologic or targeted synthetic DMARD is added after an inadequate response, particularly when poor prognostic factors such as seropositivity are present. Upfront TNF inhibitor plus methotrexate is not routine. Source: EULAR RA management recommendations 2022; ACR RA guideline 2021

corrections.notes: Current EULAR/ACR guidance favours MTX-first step-up with treat-to-target, not upfront combination therapy (TEAR, ACR 2021).
corrections.source: EULAR RA management recommendations 2022; ACR RA guideline 2021
corrections.newExplanation: Current guidelines favour starting methotrexate and escalating step by step under a treat-to-target approach, rather than upfront combination therapy. Trials such as TEAR showed that step-up achieved similar outcomes to immediate combination. Source: EULAR RA management recommendations 2022; ACR RA guideline 2021

corrections.notes: HBV serology (C) is the mandatory pre-rituximab screen (boxed warning for fatal HBV reactivation). Baseline IgG is recommended, but HBV screening is the most crucial.
corrections.source: Rituximab prescribing information (boxed warning: hepatitis B reactivation); BSR biologics guidance
corrections.newExplanation: Hepatitis B serology is mandatory before rituximab because HBV reactivation can cause fulminant hepatitis and death. Baseline immunoglobulin levels are also recommended, but HBV screening is the most crucial pre-treatment test. Source: Rituximab prescribing information (boxed warning: hepatitis B reactivation); BSR biologics guidance

corrections.notes: Aggressive fluids (250-500 mL/h) superseded: WATERFALL (NEJM 2022) showed harm, and ACG 2024 advises moderate goal-directed fluids.
corrections.source: WATERFALL trial (de-Madaria et al, NEJM 2022); ACG acute pancreatitis guideline 2024
corrections.newExplanation: The WATERFALL trial found that aggressive fluid resuscitation in acute pancreatitis increased fluid overload without improving outcomes. Current ACG guidance recommends moderate, goal-directed crystalloid resuscitation (lactated Ringer's preferred), adjusted to frequent clinical reassessment, rather than fixed high infusion rates. Source: WATERFALL trial (de-Madaria et al, NEJM 2022); ACG acute pancreatitis guideline 2024

optionEdits.after: Moderate, goal-directed crystalloid (e.g. lactated Ringer's) resuscitation with frequent reassessment

corrections.notes: EMPEROR-Preserved and DELIVER didn't significantly reduce CV death (benefit from HF hospitalisation); pooled CV death was borderline non-significant.
corrections.source: DELIVER and EMPEROR-Preserved trials; Vaduganathan et al, Lancet 2022 meta-analysis
corrections.newExplanation: In HFpEF, SGLT2 inhibitors reduce the composite of cardiovascular death or heart failure events, driven mainly by fewer heart failure hospitalisations. Neither EMPEROR-Preserved nor DELIVER showed a significant reduction in cardiovascular death on its own. Source: DELIVER and EMPEROR-Preserved trials; Vaduganathan et al, Lancet 2022 meta-analysis

corrections.notes: Baseline 10 to max 28 ppm is an 18 ppm rise, below the >=20 ppm threshold, so the glucose test is negative.
corrections.source: North American Consensus on breath testing 2017; UEG/ESNM breath testing consensus 2022
corrections.newExplanation: A positive glucose breath test requires a hydrogen rise of at least 20 ppm above baseline within 90 minutes. Here hydrogen rose from 10 to a peak of 28 ppm, an 18 ppm increase, so the test is negative for SIBO. Source: North American Consensus on breath testing 2017; UEG/ESNM breath testing consensus 2022

corrections.notes: CSF drainage is for spinal ischaemia after aortic repair (and hydrocephalus per cited NICE), not spontaneous anterior spinal infarction. Aetiological work-up (A) is the right step; thrombolysis (B) only in selected hyperacute cases.
corrections.source: Clinical Neurology and Neurosurgery 2025 review of spinal cord infarction (linked)
corrections.newExplanation: After spontaneous anterior spinal artery infarction, the key step is a thorough search for the cause, including vascular risk factors and aortic pathology, to guide secondary prevention. CSF drainage is used for spinal ischaemia after aortic surgery and for hydrocephalus, not for spontaneous spinal infarction. Source: Clinical Neurology and Neurosurgery 2025 review of spinal cord infarction (linked)

corrections.notes: Superseded: the ACC 2022 expert consensus no longer advises routine troponin/cardiac testing for athletes recovered from mild asymptomatic-cardiac COVID-19; testing only if cardiopulmonary symptoms.
corrections.source: ACC 2022 Expert Consensus Decision Pathway on cardiovascular sequelae of COVID-19
corrections.stemFix: A 19-year-old collegiate athlete, who experienced mild COVID-19 symptoms three weeks ago, is eager to return to competitive sports. He had no cardiac symptoms during his illness. His resting ECG and echocardiogram are normal. What further cardiac assessment is recommended before he returns to play?
corrections.newExplanation: The ACC 2022 consensus pathway no longer recommends routine cardiac testing, including troponin, for athletes who had COVID-19 without cardiopulmonary symptoms. They can make a graded return to exercise, with assessment reserved for those who develop chest pain, palpitations, dyspnoea or syncope. Source: ACC 2022 Expert Consensus Decision Pathway on cardiovascular sequelae of COVID-19

optionEdits.after: No further cardiac testing; graded return to exercise

corrections.notes: Blanket restriction is outdated: AHA/ACC 2020/2024 HCM guidance and ESC 2020 sports guidelines allow shared decision-making about competitive sport after expert evaluation in low-risk asymptomatic HCM.
corrections.source: AHA/ACC HCM guideline 2020/2024; ESC sports cardiology guideline 2020
corrections.newExplanation: Blanket exclusion of athletes with HCM is no longer recommended. AHA/ACC and ESC guidance supports comprehensive evaluation and risk stratification by an expert, followed by shared decision-making, which may allow continued competitive sport in asymptomatic, lower-risk patients, with an emergency action plan in place. Source: AHA/ACC HCM guideline 2020/2024; ESC sports cardiology guideline 2020

optionEdits.after: Comprehensive risk assessment by an HCM specialist and shared decision-making about continued competitive play

corrections.notes: CAP guideline advises against routine HPV/p16 testing in non-oropharyngeal (e.g. laryngeal) SCC; p16 is a poor surrogate outside the oropharynx.
corrections.source: CAP guideline on HPV testing in head and neck carcinomas (2018)
corrections.newExplanation: CAP recommends HPV/p16 testing for oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma, but advises against routine HPV testing in non-oropharyngeal sites such as the larynx, where p16 is a poor surrogate for HPV and does not guide treatment. Source: CAP guideline on HPV testing in head and neck carcinomas (2018)

corrections.notes: Standard initial steps in SAB are echocardiography plus ID consultation (B), which improve outcomes; PET-CT is a selective adjunct, not first step.
corrections.source: IDSA/ESCMID Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia guidance
corrections.newExplanation: Initial work-up of S. aureus bacteraemia includes echocardiography to look for endocarditis and early infectious diseases consultation, which improves outcomes. FDG-PET/CT is a selective adjunct to find metastatic foci when the source is unclear or bacteraemia persists, not the first step. Source: IDSA/ESCMID Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia guidance

corrections.notes: Empirical cover for S. aureus endocarditis in an IVDU must cover MRSA (vancomycin) pending sensitivities. Ceftriaxone is inadequate, and the explanation misapplies NICE child-fever guidance.
corrections.source: IDSA MRSA guideline 2011 (linked); ESC endocarditis guideline 2023
corrections.newExplanation: In a person who injects drugs with S. aureus bacteraemia and a valve vegetation, empirical therapy must cover MRSA until susceptibilities are known, so vancomycin is appropriate. Ceftriaxone does not cover MRSA and is not a recommended anti-staphylococcal agent for endocarditis. Source: IDSA MRSA guideline 2011 (linked); ESC endocarditis guideline 2023

corrections.notes: HLA-DRB1*11:01 typing has no management value once IMNM is confirmed; ENMC recommends cancer screening in anti-HMGCR IMNM.
corrections.source: ENMC international workshop on immune-mediated necrotising myopathies 2016
corrections.newExplanation: Once anti-HMGCR immune-mediated necrotising myopathy is confirmed, cancer screening is recommended because of an association with malignancy. HLA typing adds nothing to management, and antibody titres are not monitored monthly. Source: ENMC international workshop on immune-mediated necrotising myopathies 2016

corrections.notes: Fibrinolysis is preferred only when PCI delay is expected to exceed 120 min; 110 min to cath lab at the current centre is within that window, so PPCI here is preferred.
corrections.source: ESC ACS guideline 2023; ACC/AHA STEMI guidance
corrections.newExplanation: Fibrinolysis is preferred only when primary PCI cannot be delivered within 120 minutes of diagnosis. A 110-minute delay at the current PCI-capable centre is within that window, so primary PCI there remains the preferred reperfusion strategy. Source: ESC ACS guideline 2023; ACC/AHA STEMI guidance

corrections.notes: "Triple-H"/hypervolaemia is abandoned; current guidance is euvolaemia with induced hypertension, and nimodipine is prophylactic, with angioplasty/intra-arterial vasodilators for refractory vasospasm.
corrections.source: AHA/ASA aneurysmal SAH guideline 2023; NICE NG228
corrections.newExplanation: Triple-H therapy is no longer recommended, and prophylactic hypervolaemia can cause harm. For symptomatic vasospasm, current guidance is to maintain euvolaemia and raise blood pressure, continuing nimodipine. Endovascular angioplasty or intra-arterial vasodilators are rescue options for refractory vasospasm. Source: AHA/ASA aneurysmal SAH guideline 2023; NICE NG228

optionEdits.after: Maintain euvolaemia and induce hypertension, while continuing oral nimodipine

corrections.notes: SVT within 3 cm of the SFJ is treated as DVT with therapeutic anticoagulation (~3 months). Thermal ablation in acute SVT isn't recommended.
corrections.source: CHEST antithrombotic therapy for VTE guideline 2016/2021; ESVS venous thrombosis guideline 2021
corrections.newExplanation: Superficial vein thrombosis within 3 cm of the saphenofemoral junction is managed like a DVT, with therapeutic anticoagulation, typically for about 3 months. Endovenous thermal ablation is not recommended in acute thrombosis, and bed rest is not advised. Source: CHEST antithrombotic therapy for VTE guideline 2016/2021; ESVS venous thrombosis guideline 2021

corrections.notes: Flare on tapering is usually managed by going back to the last effective tocilizumab dose. Switching class is for failure at optimal dose, which the explanation itself states.
corrections.source: EULAR recommendations for large-vessel vasculitis 2018
corrections.newExplanation: Takayasu arteritis that flares when tocilizumab is tapered, after remission on full dose, is usually controlled by returning to the last effective dose. Switching to another biologic class is for disease that is refractory despite optimal dosing. Source: EULAR recommendations for large-vessel vasculitis 2018

corrections.notes: The 33-36 C TTM target is from 2015. After TTM2 (2021), ERC/ESICM 2021-2025 and AHA recommend actively preventing fever (<=37.5 C) for >=72 h; no option matches exactly.
corrections.source: TTM2 trial (Dankiewicz et al, NEJM 2021); ERC-ESICM post-resuscitation care guidelines 2021/2025
corrections.stemFix: A 62-year-old male is admitted to the emergency department after suffering an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) due to ventricular fibrillation. Return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) was achieved after 15 minutes of CPR. He remains unconscious with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) of E1V1M3. What temperature management is recommended?
corrections.newExplanation: After the TTM2 trial showed no benefit of hypothermia at 33°C over normothermia with fever prevention, ERC-ESICM guidelines recommend continuous temperature monitoring and active prevention of fever (above 37.5°C) for at least 72 hours in patients who remain comatose after ROSC. The earlier 33-36°C target is superseded. Source: TTM2 trial (Dankiewicz et al, NEJM 2021); ERC-ESICM post-resuscitation care guidelines 2021/2025

optionEdits.after: Actively prevent fever (temperature 37.5°C or lower) for at least 72 hours

corrections.notes: Rhythm-specific 32-34/36 C targets aren't a guideline recommendation. After TTM2, guidelines recommend fever prevention (<=37.5 C) regardless of rhythm.
corrections.source: TTM2 trial (NEJM 2021); ERC-ESICM post-resuscitation care guidelines 2021/2025
corrections.newExplanation: Rhythm-specific hypothermia targets are not recommended. After TTM2, ERC-ESICM guidelines recommend actively preventing fever (above 37.5°C) for at least 72 hours in comatose survivors of cardiac arrest, whatever the initial rhythm. Deep hypothermia has no role. Source: TTM2 trial (NEJM 2021); ERC-ESICM post-resuscitation care guidelines 2021/2025

optionEdits.after: Actively prevent fever (37.5°C or lower), regardless of initial rhythm

corrections.notes: The established advantage is single-bolus administration. Tenecteplase hasn't shown consistent superior clinical efficacy (EXTEND-IA TNK showed better pre-thrombectomy reperfusion; TIMELESS was neutral vs placebo).
corrections.source: EXTEND-IA TNK (NEJM 2018); ESO guideline on intravenous thrombolysis
corrections.newExplanation: The clear practical advantage of tenecteplase is single-bolus administration, which simplifies and speeds treatment, for example before transfer for thrombectomy. Trials have shown non-inferiority to alteplase, with no consistent evidence of lower intracranial haemorrhage or superior clinical efficacy. Source: EXTEND-IA TNK (NEJM 2018); ESO guideline on intravenous thrombolysis

corrections.notes: Major surgery within 14 days (not 3 months) is the relative contraindication (AHA/ASA 2019); laparoscopic cholecystectomy 6 weeks ago doesn't preclude thrombolysis.
corrections.source: AHA/ASA acute ischaemic stroke guideline 2019
corrections.newExplanation: AHA/ASA list major surgery within the previous 14 days as a relative contraindication to thrombolysis. A laparoscopic cholecystectomy 6 weeks earlier is not a contraindication, so tenecteplase can be given per standard protocol. Source: AHA/ASA acute ischaemic stroke guideline 2019

corrections.notes: Clean minor wound with booster within 10 years needs no tetanus prophylaxis (CDC/UKHSA); immunosuppression affects TIG for tetanus-prone wounds only.
corrections.source: UKHSA Green Book chapter 30 (tetanus); CDC/ACIP tetanus wound management
corrections.newExplanation: A clean, minor wound in someone whose last tetanus booster was within 10 years needs no tetanus vaccine or immunoglobulin. Immunosuppression mainly matters for tetanus-prone wounds, where immunoglobulin may be needed. Source: UKHSA Green Book chapter 30 (tetanus); CDC/ACIP tetanus wound management

corrections.notes: Fixed targets of 2.5/3.0/3.5 come from ATA 2011. ATA 2017 recommends trimester/population-specific ranges (aim for lower half), with ~4.0 as upper limit if unavailable.
corrections.source: ATA guidelines on thyroid disease in pregnancy 2017
corrections.newExplanation: ATA 2017 replaced fixed trimester cut-offs with population- and trimester-specific TSH reference ranges. In treated hypothyroidism, aim for the lower half of the trimester-specific range, using an upper limit of about 4.0 mIU/L if local ranges are unavailable. Levothyroxine needs usually rise in pregnancy, so TSH should be checked regularly. Source: ATA guidelines on thyroid disease in pregnancy 2017

corrections.notes: Early beta-blockade is standard first-line in thyroid storm, not a pitfall; the classic sequencing error is giving iodide before a thionamide. Treating symptoms without addressing hormone excess (D) is the real pitfall.
corrections.source: ATA hyperthyroidism guideline 2016; Japan Thyroid Association/Japan Endocrine Society thyroid storm guideline 2016 (linked)
corrections.newExplanation: Thyroid storm needs multimodal treatment: a beta-blocker, a thionamide, iodide (given after the thionamide), corticosteroids and supportive care. Early beta-blockade is standard, not a pitfall. The critical error is treating only the adrenergic symptoms without addressing the excess thyroid hormone. Source: ATA hyperthyroidism guideline 2016; Japan Thyroid Association/Japan Endocrine Society thyroid storm guideline 2016 (linked)

corrections.notes: Mild TR is a non-indication, not a relative contraindication. Severe RV dysfunction (A) and severe pre-capillary PH (D) are the recognised relative contraindications to T-TEER.
corrections.source: ESC/EACTS valvular heart disease guidelines; TRILUMINATE trial eligibility criteria
corrections.newExplanation: Severe right ventricular dysfunction is a recognised relative contraindication to transcatheter tricuspid edge-to-edge repair because the RV may not tolerate the change in loading. Mild tricuspid regurgitation is simply not an indication rather than a contraindication. Source: ESC/EACTS valvular heart disease guidelines; TRILUMINATE trial eligibility criteria

corrections.notes: Atezolizumab plus nab-paclitaxel lost its TNBC indication (FDA withdrawn 2021; IMpassion131 negative). Current first-line for PD-L1+ (CPS>=10) mTNBC is pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy (KEYNOTE-355).
corrections.source: KEYNOTE-355 (Cortes et al, Lancet 2020; NEJM 2022); ESMO metastatic breast cancer guideline
corrections.stemFix: A 55-year-old woman with metastatic triple-negative breast cancer whose tumour is PD-L1 positive (CPS of 10 or more) is being considered for first-line systemic therapy. According to current evidence, what is the standard-of-care regimen?
corrections.newExplanation: For first-line treatment of PD-L1-positive (CPS 10 or more) metastatic TNBC, pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy is standard, based on KEYNOTE-355, which improved progression-free and overall survival. Atezolizumab plus nab-paclitaxel lost its TNBC indication after IMpassion131 was negative. Trastuzumab and endocrine therapy do not apply to TNBC. Source: KEYNOTE-355 (Cortes et al, Lancet 2020; NEJM 2022); ESMO metastatic breast cancer guideline

The label recommends intravenous hydration plus a uric acid-lowering agent, allopurinol, started before treatment, with rasburicase if baseline uric acid is raised. His uric acid is normal, so IV hydration and allopurinol is appropriate. Source: Venetoclax summary of product characteristics / prescribing information

corrections.notes: Standard TLS prophylaxis targets urine output of about 2 mL/kg/h (80-100 mL/m2/h), not 1.
corrections.source: Coiffier et al, J Clin Oncol 2008 TLS guidelines; BSH TLS guideline
corrections.newExplanation: TLS prophylaxis in high-risk patients uses aggressive intravenous hydration to maintain a high urine output, typically about 2 mL/kg/hour, to promote excretion of uric acid, potassium and phosphate. Source: Coiffier et al, J Clin Oncol 2008 TLS guidelines; BSH TLS guideline

corrections.notes: Rasburicase is the most effective agent for lowering uric acid in TLS. Febuxostat only prevents new urate formation, like allopurinol.
corrections.source: Coiffier et al, J Clin Oncol 2008 TLS guidelines; BSH TLS guideline
corrections.newExplanation: Rasburicase converts existing uric acid to soluble allantoin and lowers uric acid rapidly, so it is the most effective agent in established TLS with hyperuricaemia. Allopurinol and febuxostat only block new urate formation and do not reduce existing uric acid. Source: Coiffier et al, J Clin Oncol 2008 TLS guidelines; BSH TLS guideline

corrections.notes: Azithromycin for uncomplicated typhoid is given for 7 days (5-7 days in WHO/current practice). 10-14 days comes from a 1992 source about older agents.
corrections.source: WHO typhoid guidance; Parry et al typhoid reviews
corrections.newExplanation: Oral azithromycin for uncomplicated typhoid fever is usually given for about 7 days (5-7 day courses in current practice). The 10-14 day duration comes from older guidance for other antibiotics. Source: WHO typhoid guidance; Parry et al typhoid reviews

corrections.notes: Haemostatic powder needs active bleeding to work and is not appropriate for a non-bleeding visible vessel (IIa). Clips or thermal plus adrenaline are standard.
corrections.source: ESGE non-variceal upper GI haemorrhage guideline 2021
corrections.newExplanation: A non-bleeding visible vessel (Forrest IIa) should be treated with mechanical (clip) or thermal therapy, alone or combined with adrenaline injection. Haemostatic powder works only on actively bleeding lesions and is not suitable for a non-bleeding visible vessel. Source: ESGE non-variceal upper GI haemorrhage guideline 2021

corrections.notes: Penicillin allergy is irrelevant here. NICE NG109 for lower UTI in non-pregnant women is nitrofurantoin 3 days or trimethoprim 3 days (if low resistance risk); 7-day nitrofurantoin is the course for men.

A 7-day course is for men. Neither agent is a penicillin, so her penicillin allergy does not change the choice. Source: NICE NG109 lower UTI antimicrobial prescribing

corrections.notes: 2020 ASHP/IDSA consensus replaced trough targets of 15-20 with AUC-guided dosing (AUC24 400-600) because of nephrotoxicity without efficacy gain.
corrections.source: ASHP/IDSA/PIDS/SIDP vancomycin therapeutic monitoring consensus 2020
corrections.stemFix: A 68-year-old male with a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes presents with fever, chills, and a painful, erythematous lesion on his left leg. Blood cultures are drawn and subsequently grow Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). He is initiated on intravenous vancomycin. Which vancomycin dosing and monitoring strategy is recommended for MRSA bacteremia?
corrections.newExplanation: The 2020 ASHP/IDSA/PIDS/SIDP consensus recommends AUC-guided vancomycin dosing for serious MRSA infections, targeting an AUC24 of 400-600 mg·h/L (assuming an MIC of 1 mg/L), ideally using Bayesian software. Trough-only targets of 15-20 µg/mL are no longer recommended because they increase nephrotoxicity without improving efficacy. Source: ASHP/IDSA/PIDS/SIDP vancomycin therapeutic monitoring consensus 2020

corrections.notes: Standard two-cannula VV-ECMO is femoral drainage with internal jugular return (femoro-jugular) or a single dual-lumen IJ cannula; femoro-femoral is an alternative, not the standard.
corrections.source: ELSO guidance for adult venovenous ECMO
corrections.newExplanation: The standard two-cannula VV-ECMO configuration drains from the femoral vein and returns to the internal jugular vein (femoro-jugular), which limits recirculation; a single dual-lumen jugular cannula is an alternative. Femoro-femoral cannulation is possible but has more recirculation and is not the standard. Source: ELSO guidance for adult venovenous ECMO

corrections.notes: Apixaban or rivaroxaban as sole initial oral agents are now first-line (NICE NG158, ASH 2020, CHEST). Parenteral lead-in is only needed for dabigatran/edoxaban.
corrections.source: NICE NG158 venous thromboembolic diseases; ASH VTE treatment guideline 2020
corrections.newExplanation: For most patients with acute DVT, a DOAC is first-line. Apixaban or rivaroxaban can be started alone without parenteral lead-in, whereas dabigatran and edoxaban need initial LMWH. Parenteral anticoagulation with warfarin is reserved for patients who cannot take a DOAC. Source: NICE NG158 venous thromboembolic diseases; ASH VTE treatment guideline 2020

corrections.notes: Ribavirin benefit in Lassa fever is greatest when started within the first 6 days of illness (McCormick 1986). A 10-day threshold is unsupported.
corrections.source: McCormick et al, NEJM 1986; UKHSA/WHO Lassa fever guidance
corrections.newExplanation: Intravenous ribavirin for Lassa fever is most effective when started within the first 6 days of illness, as shown by McCormick et al. It should be started on clinical suspicion without waiting for PCR confirmation. Source: McCormick et al, NEJM 1986; UKHSA/WHO Lassa fever guidance

corrections.notes: ASH 2018 and CHEST advise against routine extended post-discharge prophylaxis in acutely ill medical patients because bleeding offsets VTE benefit (APEX, MAGELLAN, MARINER). The keyed 10-day extension for high-risk patients is unsupported.
corrections.source: ASH VTE prophylaxis guideline for medical patients 2018; CHEST guidance
corrections.newExplanation: ASH and CHEST advise against routine extended VTE prophylaxis after hospital discharge in acutely ill medical patients, including after ICU stays, because the extra bleeding risk offsets the reduction in VTE seen in trials such as APEX, MAGELLAN and MARINER. Source: ASH VTE prophylaxis guideline for medical patients 2018; CHEST guidance
